node.label: Sheila Fitzpatrick
node.description: A historian of the Soviet Union and of Stalinism from below. In ‘Revisionism in Retrospect’ (2008) she gives a participant’s account of how social historians of the 1970s and 1980s challenged political scientists’ totalitarian model, crediting revisionism with an appreciation of contingency and a new approach to power and to the interplay of government and society. Stalin’s Peasants: Resistance and Survival in the Russian Village after Collectivization (1994) and Everyday Stalinism: Ordinary Life in Extraordinary Times (1999) carry that social history into village and city. In a comparative chapter with Alf Lüdtke on Nazism and Stalinism, she treats Hannah Arendt’s thesis of social atomization as a question for research: social bonds were broken but also remade, and participation involved people’s emotional investments.
